en: The Jātaka:
Great Section, Chapter on the Mūgapakkha (The Dumb and Paralysed)
2. The Mahājanaka Jātaka:
“Who is this that, seeing no shore, strives in the midst of the ocean?”
“Knowing what purpose do you exert yourself so intensely?
“Having reflected upon the conduct of the world,”
And because of my exertion, O deity,
I struggled in the midst of the ocean,
not seeing the shore.
“In that which is deep and immeasurable,
whose further shore is not seen—
vain is your human effort.”
"You will die without having reached [your goal].
"He is free from debt to his kinsmen,
to the gods, and to his father."
Performing the duties of a man,
he does not regret it later.
That action which cannot be led across [to its result]—
Fruitless is the exertion that results only in weariness;
what purpose is there in striving against one for whom Death has already descended?
“O deity, one who, having understood that the beyond is utterly unleadable,
does not protect his own life— ”
If he should neglect it, O deity, one might know [the consequence] regarding the fruit of his intention in this world.
They perform actions that may or may not succeed;
the fruit of action is visible here and now.
"Surely you see them, O deity?
I recognize others, and I see him too, standing right here."
Thus I shall strive,
according to my power and according to my strength,
going to the further shore of the ocean.
"Whose is this manly deed? "It is yours,
who, while this flood has thus set in,
[stand] in the immeasurable great ocean."
Endowed with effort in the Dhamma,
you do not sink because of your actions;
therefore, go right there.
Wherever your mind finds delight—
whether at the rising of the sun or at its setting— that is a treasure.
A treasure within, a treasure without,
neither within nor without is the treasure.
A great treasure lies in ascending.
Furthermore, at the foot of the tree there is a treasure;
in the four great *sāla* trees,
there is a treasure extending for a league in every direction.
A great treasure is at the tips of the teeth, and at the tips of the hair;
a great treasure is at the tips of trees.
These are the sixteen great treasures;
the couch with a thousandfold strength,
and through the propitiation of Sīvalā.
A wise person should indeed aspire and not become despondent;
for I see myself as such.
As I wished, so it came to pass.
A wise person should indeed aspire; he should not become despondent.
I see myself as one who has been pulled from the water onto dry land;
let the man indeed exert himself.
The wise person should not become despondent;
I see myself now exactly as I had wished.
A wise person should indeed strive and not become despondent;
for I see myself [in this state].
Like water washed up onto dry land,
even a wise person who has been brought to suffering should not cut off hope for the arrival of happiness.
For many contacts, both harmful and beneficial,
lead to death even without being anticipated;
and what was not thought of also comes to pass.
Even what is thought of perishes;
for wealth does not arise from mere thought,
whether for a woman or for a man.
“Indeed, sir, King Disampati was ancient and sovereign over all;
today he does not even listen to music.”
He does not set his mind on song,
nor on deer, nor on the park;
he does not gaze even at the swans.
“Like a mute one, sitting in silence,
he does not instruct on the goal.
“Those who desire happiness, whose conduct is secluded,”
Ceased from killing and binding—
who today in the monastery are there,
both young and old?
The wise have transcended the forest of existence;
homage to those great seers who,
in a world full of striving, have gone beyond.
They dwell seeking human happiness.
Having cut through the net of Death—
the strong, widespread snare of the deceiver—
Since they depart with their attachments severed,
who can follow their path?
When shall I [return] to the prosperous Mithilā?
Divided and measured out in portions;
when shall it be that I have abandoned this and gone forth into homelessness?
When shall I renounce Mithilā, so prosperous,
vast, and radiant on every side,
and go forth into homelessness?
When will that time ever come?
When shall I [return] to Mithilā,
the prosperous city with its many walls and gate-towers?
Having abandoned it, I shall go forth;
when will that ever be?
When shall I [leave] Mithilā, so prosperous?
Having abandoned this fortress with its strong towers and ramparts,
when will I go forth into homelessness?
When indeed will that time come?
When shall I renounce Mithilā, so prosperous,
well-laid out with great highways,
and go forth into homelessness?
When will that time ever come?
When shall I see Mithilā, prosperous,
with its well-laid-out market streets?
Having abandoned [it], I shall go forth;
when will that ever be?
When shall I [leave] Mithilā, so prosperous?
Oppressed by cattle, carts,
and chariots— when will it be that I shall renounce these and go forth?
When shall I renounce Mithilā, so prosperous and garlanded with parks and groves,
and go forth into homelessness?
When will that time ever come?
When shall I [return to] Mithilā, so prosperous and garlanded with gardens and groves?
Having abandoned [it], I shall go forth;
when will that ever be?
When shall I [leave] Mithilā, so prosperous?
Having abandoned this palace garlanded with groves,
when will I go forth into homelessness?
When indeed will that time come?
"When shall I build the prosperous city of Mithilā,
with its triple walls and royal palaces, out of joy?"
When will that time come when,
having abandoned [this life],
I shall go forth under the illustrious King of Videha?
When shall I, having abandoned my flourishing kingdom, rich and protected by righteousness,
go forth into homelessness?
When will that time ever come?
When shall I [rule] over the prosperous Vedehas,
who are unconquerable and protected by Dhamma?
Having abandoned it, I shall go forth;
when will that time ever be?
When will I [leave] the delightful inner palace?
Divided and measured out into portions—
when shall it be that I have abandoned this and gone forth into homelessness?
When shall I renounce the delightful inner palace,
plastered with lime and clay,
and go forth into homelessness?
When will that time ever come?
When shall I [enter] the delightful inner palace,
fragrant and enchanting?
Having abandoned [it], I shall go forth;
when will that ever be?
When shall I [dwell] in gabled houses?
When [the world] has been divided and measured out into portions—
when will that time come when I shall renounce it all and go forth?
When shall I renounce my gabled house,
plastered with fine lime,
and go forth into homelessness?
When will that time ever come?
When shall I dwell in a gabled chamber,
pure-scented and delightful?
"Having abandoned [this life], I shall go forth;
when will that ever be?
When shall I [dwell] in gabled houses?"
Anointed with a little sandalwood paste;
when shall that time come when I shall renounce the world and go forth?
When shall I leave behind my golden couch,
spread with woolen blankets and embroidered cloth,
and go forth into homelessness?
When will that time ever come?
When shall I lie upon a jeweled couch,
spread with woolen rugs and covered with fine cloth?
Having abandoned [these], I shall go forth;
when will that ever be?
When shall I [wear] cotton and silk?
And fine linen and cotton garments;
having abandoned these, I shall go forth—
when will that time ever be?
When shall I [bathe] in a delightful lotus pond,
resounding with the cries of ruddy geese and covered with mandārava flowers?
And with lotuses and water-lilies;
having abandoned them, I shall go forth—
when will that ever be?
When shall I [ride] upon a herd of elephants,
adorned with every ornament—
those noble tuskers with golden girths?
When he had mounted his golden-hued elephant,
led by village chiefs holding spears and goads in their hands;
Having abandoned [it], I shall go forth;
when will that ever be?
When shall I, in the Assagumba grove...
Adorned with every ornament,
like noble Sindhu horses of pure breed, swift in their course.
When the village headmen, bearing their spears and bows, have mounted [their chariots],
I shall abandon them and go forth into homelessness.
When will that time ever be?
When shall I [see] the chariot-arrays,
armored and with banners raised?
And furthermore, on the island of Ceylon,
there were two tigers adorned with every ornament,
mounted by village chiefs.
When there are armored men with bows in their hands,
when will it be that I shall renounce the world, having abandoned [this life]?
When shall I [ride] in a golden chariot,
equipped and with banners raised high;
and likewise on islands and in forests of wild beasts?
Adorned with every ornament,
mounted by village chiefs clad in armor and holding bows in their hands.
Having abandoned [them], I shall go forth;
when indeed will that be?
When shall I [renounce] the chariots and horses?
When he was armored, with his banner raised high—
whether on the island or at Veyyaggha,
adorned with every ornament.
When the village headmen, clad in armor and with bows in hand, have mounted [their horses],
I shall abandon [this life] and go forth into homelessness.
When will that time ever come?
When shall I [see] horse-chariots equipped with armor and raised banners?
Furthermore, in the island of Ceylon,
there were two tigers adorned with every ornament,
mounted by village chiefs.
When there are armored men with bows in their hands,
when will that time come when I can renounce the world, having abandoned [all this]?
When shall I [be present] at Oṭṭharatha,
when it is armored and its banners raised;
and likewise at Dīpa and at Veyyaggha?
Adorned with every ornament,
mounted by village chiefs who were clad in armor and held bows in their hands.
Having abandoned [them], I shall go forth;
when will that ever be? When shall I [ride] in a chariot drawn by oxen?
When he is armored, with his banner raised high—
whether on the island or in the Veyyaggha forest—
adorned with every ornament.
When the village headmen, clad in armor and with bows in hand, have mounted [their horses],
I shall abandon [this life] and go forth into homelessness.
When will that time ever come?
When shall I see the chariot of the Ageless,
armored and with its banner raised high?
Furthermore, on the island of Ceylon,
there were two tigers adorned with every ornament,
mounted by village chiefs.
When there are armored men with bows in their hands,
when will it be that I shall renounce the world, having abandoned [this life]?
When shall I [be like] Meṇḍaratha,
with his armor fastened and his banner raised;
and likewise [like] Dīpa and Veyyaggha?
Adorned with every ornament,
mounted by village chiefs who were armored and held bows in their hands.
Having abandoned [them], I shall go forth;
when will that ever be?
When shall I [ride] upon deer-chariots?
When he was armored, with his banner raised high—
whether on the island or at Veyyaggha—
adorned with every ornament.
When the village headmen, clad in armor and with bows in hand, have mounted [their horses],
I shall abandon [this life] and go forth.
When will that time ever come?
When shall I [see] those mounted on elephants,
adorned with every ornament?
O hero wearing blue armor,
holding a spear and a goad in your hands,
having abandoned [the world], I shall go forth.
When will that time ever come?
When shall I [give] horse-riders adorned with every ornament?
O hero wearing blue armor,
bearing a bow of reeds,
having abandoned [the world], I shall go forth.
When will that time ever come?
When shall I [see] those mounted on chariots,
adorned with every ornament?
O hero clad in blue armor,
holding a bow and a quiver—
having abandoned you, I shall go forth.
When will that time ever come?
When shall I [see] the archers,
adorned with every ornament?
O hero wearing blue armor,
holding a bow and a quiver—
having abandoned you, I shall go forth.
When will that time ever come?
When shall I [see] the princes,
adorned with every ornament?
Having abandoned the hero clad in variegated armor,
wearing golden earrings,
I shall go forth into homelessness.
When will that time ever come?
When shall I [dwell] among the assembly of noble ones,
who are disciplined and adorned with virtue?
Having abandoned my limbs anointed with yellow sandalwood and wearing the finest Kāsī cloth,
I shall go forth into homelessness.
When will that time ever come? When shall I,
amidst my circle of ministers all adorned with every ornament, [behold him]?
While the hero wearing yellow armor proceeds ahead garlanded,
I shall abandon [the world] and go forth.
When will that time ever come?
When shall I [be surrounded by] seven hundred wives,
all adorned with every kind of ornament?
Having abandoned [them], I shall go forth;
when will that ever come to pass?
When shall I [leave] my seven hundred wives?
With clear perception and slender waist,
when shall I ever be able to renounce it all and go forth?
When shall I, having abandoned my seven hundred wives who are obedient and speak so sweetly,
go forth into homelessness?
When will that time ever come?
When shall I obtain a bronze vessel weighing a hundred palas,
adorned with a hundred royal designs in gold?
Having abandoned [them], I shall go forth;
when will that ever be?
When will the herds of elephants [ever leave me]?
Adorned with every ornament,
these elephant-riders had golden girths and were clad in garments of gold brocade.
Mounted by village chiefs with spears and goads in their hands,
they will not follow me as I proceed.
When will that time ever come?
When will the herd of horses, adorned with every ornament, bring me [back]?
Like noble Sindhu horses, swift in their course,
they are mounted by village leaders.
When will that time come when those who bear the rod of punishment shall no longer pursue me?
When indeed will the army of chariots,
armored and with banners raised—
those adorned with elephants and tigers— [come to me]?
Adorned with every ornament,
they were mounted by village chiefs who carried bows in their hands and wore armor.
When will that time come when they will no longer follow me?
When will my golden chariots—
They were armored with raised banners;
some were adorned with lamps and others with tiger skins,
all decorated with every kind of ornament.
Mounted by village chiefs,
armed with bows and clad in armor—
these will not follow after me as I depart.
When will that time ever come?
When will the chariots of the Sañjaya clan,
armored and with banners raised, [come to my aid]?
There were also women from Dīpa and Veyyaggha,
adorned with every ornament,
mounted upon village headmen.
When will that time come when those armored men with bows in their hands will no longer pursue me?
When indeed will horse-drawn chariots arrive for me—
fully equipped, with banners raised high,
adorned with leopards and tigers?
Adorned with every ornament,
they were mounted by village chiefs who bore bows in their hands and wore armor.
When will that time come when they no longer follow me?
When will they turn back from the chariot-path?
They were armored with raised banners;
some were adorned with lamps and others with tiger skins,
all decorated with every kind of ornament.
Mounted by village chiefs,
armed with bows and clad in armor—
these will not follow my chariot.
When will that time ever come?
When will there be for me chariots drawn by oxen,
harnessed and with banners raised high?
There were also women from Dīpa and Veyyaggha,
adorned with every ornament,
mounted upon the village chiefs.
When will that time come when those with bows in hand and clad in armor shall no longer pursue me?
When indeed shall I, armored, with banners raised high, stand upon chariots that are ageless—
whether those made of ivory or even those adorned with tiger skins?
Adorned with every ornament,
they were mounted by village leaders who carried bows in their hands and wore armor.
When will that time come when they will no longer follow me?
When will my carriage of rams [be left behind]?
They were armored with raised banners;
some were adorned with lamps and others with tiger skins,
all decorated with every kind of ornament.
Mounted by village chiefs,
armed with bows and clad in armor—
they will not follow after me as I go to the machine.
When will that time ever come?
When will the deer-chariots,
armored and with banners raised, [come for me]?
There were also women from Dīpa and Veyyaggha,
adorned with every ornament,
mounted upon their village chiefs.
When will that time come when those armored men with bows in their hands shall no longer pursue me?
When indeed will the elephant-riders,
adorned with every ornament,
brave and wearing blue turbans, [come to me]?
When will that time come when those with goads and hooks in their hands no longer follow me as I go?
When indeed will horsemen,
adorned with every ornament,
brave warriors wearing blue turbans, [come to me]?
Bearing the bow of mindfulness,
when will that time come when they no longer follow after me?
When indeed will those brave chariot-warriors,
adorned with every ornament and wearing blue turbans, [come to me]?
When will that time come when those with bows in hand and quivers shall no longer pursue me?
When indeed will archers,
adorned with every ornament,
brave heroes wearing blue turbans, [come for me]?
With bows in hand and quivers at their sides,
when will it be that they no longer follow after me?
When indeed will the princes,
adorned with all ornaments,
wearing variegated garments, and heroic, [come to me]?
Wearing golden earrings—
when will that time come when they no longer follow after me?
When indeed will the noble hosts,
eloquent and adorned,
their limbs anointed with yellow sandalwood, [approach me]?
Wearing the finest garments of Kāsi,
when will that time come when they no longer follow after me?
When indeed will the assembly of ministers,
adorned with every ornament,
brave and wearing yellow garments, [approach me]?
When I am walking ahead of the garland-bearers,
when will that time come when they no longer follow after me?
When indeed will my seven hundred wives,
adorned with every ornament,
no longer follow me as I go?
When will that time ever come?
When will those seven hundred wives of mine—
well-proportioned and slender-waisted— be mine?
When will that time come when they will no longer follow me?
When will my seven hundred wives [no longer follow me]?
When will that time come when even those who were obedient and spoke so sweetly will no longer follow me?
When shall I, having taken up the bowl,
shaven-headed and clad in the outer robe,
go about for alms?
When will that time ever be?
When shall I [take up] discarded rags from the great highway?
"I shall wear the saṅghāṭī robe;
when indeed will that be?
When, during a seven-day torrential rain,"
My robe is soaked and my garment is wet;
when will it be possible for me to go out for alms?
When, having gone everywhere,
from tree to tree and forest to forest,
shall I go forth without longing?
When will that time ever be? When shall I,
having abandoned fear and terror, dwell among the rugged mountain passes?
"I shall go alone;
when will that time ever be?
When, like a lute-player, shall I..."
When shall I straighten my mind, which is as delightful as a well-strung bowstring?
When indeed will that come to pass?
When shall I, like a wheelwright cutting away at a sandal,
sever the fetter of sensual desire?
Those who were celestial and those who were human—
those seven hundred wives,
adorned with every ornament.
Raising their arms and crying out,
"Why will you abandon us?", those seven hundred wives—
With slender waists and beautiful forms,
they raised their arms and cried out,
"Why will you abandon us?"
And those seven hundred wives,
obedient and sweet-spoken,
raised their arms and wailed aloud.
"Why will you abandon us?
And those seven hundred wives,
adorned with every ornament, [spoke thus].
Having abandoned the path of prosperity, the king,
preceded by his renunciation,
left behind those seven hundred wives.
With clear perception and slender waist,
the king, having abandoned his prosperity,
went forth, preceded by the renunciant life.
And those seven hundred wives,
obedient and sweet-spoken—
the king abandoned them all and fled from his prosperity.
Honored for his going forth,
having abandoned a bronze bowl weighing a hundred palas and a golden one adorned with a hundred stripes;
He took up a clay bowl;
that was his second consecration.
"Terrifying are the flames, like fire—"
The treasuries are burning away in every part:
silver and gold,
pearls, and many beryl stones.
Jewels, conch shells, pearls, cloth,
yellow sandalwood,
antelope skins, and ivory articles.
There is much iron and black steel;
come, O King, turn back,
lest this wealth of yours be destroyed.”
“Extremely happy indeed we live,
for us there is nothing at all;
even while Mithilā is burning, [we are unshaken].”
"Nothing of mine was burned.
"Wildernesses have arisen that are destroying your kingdom."
"Come, O King, turn back;
do not let this kingdom perish.
"We indeed live most happily," [he replied].
For us there is nothing at all;
while the kingdom was being plundered,
nothing of mine was taken away.
"Truly we live in great happiness,
we who possess nothing;
we shall subsist on joy."
“Like the Ābhassara devas.
“What is this great sound?
What game is being played in the village?”
“Ascetic, we ask you this:
where has this multitude gone?
“Leaving me behind as I departed,” he replied.
There this person has come,
striving to cross beyond the boundary for the sake of attaining the state of a Sage.
“Why do you question one who knows, as he goes along with his joys?
Do not think, ‘I have crossed over.’”
While maintaining this body,
there are indeed many obstacles to that which is beyond crossing over.
“Who indeed is my adversary,
as I dwell in this way— he who,
whether seen or unseen, does not obstruct me?”
One should not long for sensual pleasures.
“Drowsiness, lethargy, yawning,
discontent, and drowsiness from overeating;”
“Many indeed are the obstacles that dwell within the body.
“It is truly a blessing for me, sir, that you have come.”
The brahmin instructs;
O brahmin, I ask you this very thing:
who indeed are you, dear sir?
“Nārada is my name,
though I am known as Kassapa;
I have come into your presence, sir.”
It is good to associate with the virtuous.
May all that joy of yours,
and your dwelling, come to fruition.
Fill whatever is deficient with patience and tranquility;
extend yourself toward those who are humble.
Raise yourself up and stretch forth;
having honored kamma, knowledge, and the Dhamma,
go forth as a wanderer.
Having abandoned many elephants and horses,
cities and provinces, O Father,
I have gone forth into homelessness.
found delight in a skull.
I wonder, are your countrymen,
friends, ministers, and kinsmen—
“O Janaka, they were indeed wicked;
why did you not disapprove of them?
“O Migājina, never at all.”
Never at any time have I conquered a kinsman by unrighteousness,
nor have my kinsmen ever conquered me.
Having seen the world’s course,
being devoured and turned to mud;
there they are slain and there they are bound.
Wherein the worldling sinks;
having made this my simile,
I am a mendicant clad in a deer-skin.
“Who indeed is your Blessed One as teacher?
Whose is this well-spoken word?
For neither the world-system nor knowledge—”
Having renounced [worldly life], O bull among charioteers,
they speak of the ascetic life as it is lived,
according to which there is a transcendence of suffering.
Never at any time have I seen, among those who wear deer-skins,
any ascetic or brahmin whatsoever—
Having paid homage, I entered.
"Moving with great majesty, radiant with glory,"
While songs were being sung,
while lutes were being played, and amidst the resounding of musical instruments and cymbals,
While I was concentrated in the Sammatāla absorption,
I saw a deer-skin, a madda flower,
a ripe mango, and a curtain beyond.
While being struck by men,
those creatures desiring flesh, I,
casting aside that glory, [departed].
Having descended and put on a deer-skin,
I approached the foot of a mango tree,
both one that bore fruit and one that was fruitless.
Having seen one mango fruit that was destroyed,
pierced, and rendered sapless,
he then [saw] another mango.
Blue-hued and heart-pleasing.
Even so, surely we too are under the sway of many thorns, O Lord!
"Enemies will slay us,
just as the mango tree was slain when it bore fruit;
even a leopard is killed for its skin."
An elephant is slain by its tusks;
those who possess wealth destroy others through that very wealth—
[but not one who is] homeless and free from attachment.
"The mango tree with fruit and the one without fruit—
both of them are my teachers.
"All people are distressed;”
"The king has gone forth!"—
thus cried the elephant riders, the cavalrymen,
the charioteers, and the foot soldiers.
Having comforted the people,
having set aside his disguise,
and having established his son in the kingdom,
“Then you will go forth later.
“I have four [groups]: countryfolk, friends, ministers, and kinsmen;”
The Videhan princes exist,
Dīghāvu the increaser of the realm;
they shall exercise sovereignty.
In Mithilā, Pajāpati said:
"Come, I shall instruct you in that which accords with my word."
You exercise sovereignty,
yet you commit much evil and misconduct through body,
speech, and mind.
By which you go to a miserable destination.
Sustain yourself with alms-food given by others and prepared by others;
that is the way of the wise.”
“Even one who does not eat at the fourth mealtime might die of hunger like an exhausted woman;
yet it is better than that one should consume impure, un-Aryan food.”
“A true man in the form of a clansman would not associate with such a person;
this is not good, this is not right, for you,
O father, are eating the leavings of a dog.”
“Moreover, Sīvālī, that which has been relinquished by a householder or even a dog is not unfit to be eaten for me;
whatever wealth has been righteously acquired here— ”
"All that food is said to be without fault.
"In the case of young girls, Upasenī,
who are constantly adorned with necklaces,"
“Why does one of your arms grow, while the other arm of yours does not grow?
“In this hand of mine, O ascetic,” he replied.
Two lutes are joined together;
a sound arises from their union,
for that is the destiny of the second.
"In this hand of mine, O ascetic,
there is a single cloak fastened;
it is without a companion and knows no other."
He stands as if he has become a sage.
When a second person enters into dispute,
with whom shall the one [first] person dispute?
“O Sīvalī, listen to this discourse, for you who desire heaven, let your mind be inclined toward solitude.”
It was proclaimed by the maiden:
"Pesī shall revile me;
such is the destiny of a second [offense]."
This is a forked path, O Bhaddā,
trodden by various people;
choose one of these for yourself.
Furthermore, once more:
Do not say to me, "Be my husband," nor again, "I am your wife."
Speaking thus, they approached the pillar at the gateway of the city,
where an arrow-maker was working.
When the time for the meal had arrived,
there the fletcher had prepared a single straight shaft.
Closing one eye,
he looks with the other askance:
"In this way you see well enough," they say.
O fletcher, listen to me:
why is it that you have drawn back one eye and look crooked with the other?
“O ascetic, by means of two eyes,
it appears as vast as the sky;
yet without having reached the supreme mark, [it remains so].”
It is permissible for the sake of playfulness.
But when one has squinted one eye and looks askance with the other;
Having attained the supreme state,
one is fit for rectitude.
When the second person has fallen into dispute,
Who will dispute with whom?
Therefore, you who desire heaven,
let single-mindedness be pleasing to you.
“Listen, Sīvalī, to this discourse as it was understood by the fowler:
‘You have censured me because of the meat-ball.’”
That is indeed the destination of the second.
This is the forked path, O Bhaddā, which has been followed by beings on earth.
Of these, you take one;
I shall take another later.
Do not say to me, "Be my husband."
"Nor am I your wife again;
O Sīvalī, you have been wedded to muñja grass and reeds— dwell alone."
The Mahājanaka Jātaka, the second.
